title: Supreme Court: Rotating Reserved Seats Is for Parliament to Decide, Not Courts
excerpt: A bench led by Chief Justice Surya Kant refused to interfere with an Allahabad High Court ruling upholding Section 9(1)(c) of the Delimitation Act, holding that neither the Constitution nor the Act requires reserved constituencies to rotate.
body:
• The Supreme Court on Wednesday rejected a plea for mandatory rotation of constituencies reserved for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes, holding that the question is a matter of legislative policy for Parliament.
  • The bench of Chief Justice Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V. Mohana refused to interfere with the Allahabad High Court judgment upholding Section 9(1)(c) of the Delimitation Act, 2002, which places reserved seats where the SC or ST population share is comparatively large.
  • Neither Articles 330 and 332 of the Constitution nor the Delimitation Act contains a rotation requirement — unlike Articles 243D and 243T, which do mandate rotation for panchayat and municipal seats.
  • The petitioner, a voter from the 191-Kadipur assembly constituency in Uttar Pradesh, which has been reserved for SC candidates since 2002, was left free to approach elected representatives and build consensus for a change in the law.

Whether India reserved parliamentary and assembly seats should move from constituency to constituency is a question for lawmakers, not judges. The Supreme Court on Wednesday rejected a plea seeking mandatory rotation of seats reserved for Scheduled Castes (SCs) and Scheduled Tribes (STs) in Parliament and state assemblies, holding that the issue falls within the legislative domain and cannot be directed by courts, according to Live Law.

What the court actually decided

The bench of Chief Justice of India Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V. Mohana was hearing a challenge to Section 9(1)(c) of the Delimitation Act, 2002, which requires reserved constituencies to be located, as far as practicable, in areas where the proportion of the SC or ST population is comparatively large. The Allahabad High Court had upheld that provision and refused to order rotation; the Supreme Court saw no reason to differ.

https://x.com/LiveLawIndia/status/2117909938781749637

"The High Court has turned down the case observing that although ideally rotation ought to be followed, such a recourse cannot be directed by the court and it is in the ambit of the Parliament. We see no ground to take a different view."

— Supreme Court order, as reported by Live Law

During the hearing, the bench made the boundary explicit: the court can strike down a provision or read one down, but it cannot rewrite the Constitution or a statute by inserting a rotation requirement that Articles 330 and 332 and the Delimitation Act do not contain, Verdictum reported.

Why the petitioner wanted rotation

The case came from Jagdish Singh, a voter in the 191-Kadipur assembly constituency in Sultanpur district, Uttar Pradesh. Kadipur has been reserved for SC candidates since 2002, and his counsel argued the constituency had remained reserved for decades while the same reservation principle is applied by rotation in local bodies. The contrast is real: Articles 243D and 243T of the Constitution expressly provide for rotation of reserved seats in panchayats and municipalities. For Parliament and assemblies, Articles 330 and 332 fix the number of reserved seats in proportion to population but say nothing about which seats or rotation — a gap the Allahabad High Court, in its June 22, 2026 judgment, held is filled by Parliament power under Article 327 to make election law.

What happens now

The petition was disposed of with liberty for the petitioner to approach public representatives and build consensus for legislation introducing rotation, relying on the reservation exercise carried out by the Delimitation Commission in 2008. In practice, that means the argument moves to Parliament, where rotation would have to be written into delimitation law. Until a legislature does that, the seats reserved at the last delimitation stay reserved, on the population-share test the courts have now upheld twice.
